extracted.intended_audience: readers and researchers interested in the history of advertising (historians, students, general readers)
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts and comments on 18th-century British newspaper advertisements and the practices/expectations they reveal (e.g., theatre notices, product ads, rewards, service hiring). The page is a book excerpt illustrating advertising conventions and implied standards of the period.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authorized publication of theatre advertisements
rubrics_metrics.description: “The Managers of Drury Lane think it proper to give notice that Advertisements of their Plays by their authority are published only in this Paper and the Daily Courant, and that the Publishers of all other Papers who presume to insert Advertisements of the same Plays, can do it only by some surreptitious intelligence or hearsay...”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Theatre managers restrict which newspapers may publish authorised play advertisements to control accuracy and publicity. Unauthorized insertions are described as coming from surreptitious intelligence or hearsay and are treated as improper.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accuracy in play titles and parts (avoid misrepresentation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Publishers of other papers who insert play adverts without authority frequently 'commit gross Errors, as mentioning one Play for another, falsely representing the Parts, etc. to the misinformation of the Town and the great detriment of the said Theatre.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advertisements for performances should correctly state the play title and cast/parts; misrepresentation is explicitly criticised and seen as harmful to theatres.

rubrics_metrics.name: Product advertisement: price and full directions
rubrics_metrics.description: R. Gibson's advertisement: he 'sells this useful composition at 5s. an ounce, with such full directions that any Person may use it themselves.' The copy also claims rapid and harmless removal of hair.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Product ads provide explicit pricing and claim to include complete usage directions so buyers can self-apply; they also make specific efficacy and safety claims (e.g., removes hair 'in half a minute' 'without the least hurt to the finest Skin').

rubrics_metrics.name: Minimum quantity and exclusive availability stated
rubrics_metrics.description: Gibson: 'No less a quantity of the composition can be had than one Ounce, nor of the preparation or paste than one Pot.' Also: 'to be had of him and nowhere else in England, next door to the Golden Star... N.B. — Gibson in gold Letters over the Door.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advertisements specify minimum sale quantities, exclusivity of vendor/location, and signage information to help customers identify the seller.

rubrics_metrics.name: Event advertisement names performers and venue preparations
rubrics_metrics.description: Notice: 'A Te Deum, composed by Mr Handel ... will be performed by Mr Beard, and a proper Band of the best performers, both vocal and instrumental. The Hall will be properly aired.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Event notices name headline performers, assert the quality of the band/performers, and sometimes include venue readiness (e.g., airing the hall) to reassure patrons about the experience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subscription/reward terms and prosecution expense promises
rubrics_metrics.description: Chelsea subscription notice: enumerates rewards ('For every Robbery... Ten Pounds. For ... stealing any Horse... Five Pounds. For ... Theft ... in any Garden ... Forty Shillings') and promises to 'pay and discharge the whole, or such Part of the Expence of such Prosecution ... as ... shall judge reasonable,' with rewards payable 'in fourteen Days after Conviction.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reward adverts specify amounts for specified offences, conditions for payment (conviction), timeframes for payment, and a pledge to contribute to prosecution costs subject to subscribers' judgment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Service adverts require explicit, honest inquiries and promise discretion
rubrics_metrics.description: Example: 'The greatest Delicacy, Discretion, and most Inviolable Secrecy may be depended on. Therefore ... the Advertiser is determined to answer such Letters only that appear explicit and satisfactory, with the Principal's Name and Place of Abode.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Providers of sensitive services demand explicit, verifiable correspondence (names and addresses) before responding and advertise confidentiality as a selling point.

rubrics_metrics.name: Employment/hiring adverts specify qualifications, age limits and exclusions
rubrics_metrics.description: Female companion ad: 'She must also possess the usual accomplishments required by a good Education; know something of Music, have an agreeable Voice, and a genteel Person, not under twenty nor above the age of twenty-five years. ... No kept Mistress or lady of Pleasure need apply.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hiring adverts set specific skill, age and moral/exclusionary criteria for applicants and explicitly instruct certain classes not to apply.

rubrics_metrics.name: Service pricing and satisfaction guarantee
rubrics_metrics.description: Barber's shop ad: 'the people can have their Hair cut for 2d., dressed for 3d., and be shaved for 1d. ... Bleeding 3d., drawing teeth 4d. ... The people may depend on being served immediately and well in every respect. No satisfaction, no pay.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Commercial service adverts provide itemised prices, assert prompt and quality service, and may offer a 'no satisfaction, no pay' guarantee as a trust signal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement for real names/residences and deposits for certain enquiries
rubrics_metrics.description: Several notices: 'Only letters with real names and residencies will be regarded.' 'It is requested that honest Initials be sent, else the deposit of two shillings and sixpence is useless.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advertisers frequently require truthful identification (real names/addresses) and sometimes small deposits to process inquiries or to deter frivolous responses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Managers' responses to adverse criticism (punitive measures)
rubrics_metrics.description: Commentary: 'Managers of the present day never object to anything but adverse criticism in a newspaper, and this affects them in various ways. ... sometimes the advertisement of the theatre is summarily stopped, at others the usual first-night privilege is suspended, and ... letters have been written and published showing how utterly biassed the criticism has been.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Theatrical managers tolerated positive publicity but would retaliate against negative press by withdrawing advertising privileges, suspending first-night privileges, or publicly accusing critics of bias.
